UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Southern Indiana Gas and Electric                               )
Company                                                         )
                                                                )           Docket No. EL26-38-000
v.                                                              )
                                                                )
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                  )


     REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF THE OFFICE OF THE ILLINOIS ATTORNEY
                              GENERAL

        Pursuant to Rule 713 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.713, and Section 313 of the

Federal Power Act (“FPA”), 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a), the People of the State of Illinois, by its Attorney

General, Kwame Raoul (the "People" or “IL OAG”), respectfully submit this Request for

Rehearing of the Commission’s March 19 Order in the above-captioned docket. The IL OAG filed

an intervention in this proceeding and filed comments on January 26, 2026. 1

I.      INTRODUCTION

        On December 23, 2025, the DOE issued the Culley Order (202-25-13) 2 to MISO and

Centerpoint Energy (aka “Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company,” “CenterPoint Energy

Indiana South,” “SIGE,” or the “Company”), pursuant to 202(c) of the Federal Power Act. 3 The

DOE Order directs MISO, in coordination with Centerpoint Energy to ensure Unit 2 of the F.B.

Culley Generating Station (“Culley Unit 2”) remains available for operation during the period of

the DOE Order (December 23, 2025, through March 23, 2026). The DOE Order is being



1
  Southern Indian Gas and Electric Company. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. EL26-38-000,
Motion to Intervene and Comments of the Office of the Illinois Attorney General (filed January 26, 2026).
2
  U.S. Department of Energy, Order No. 202-25-13 (December 23, 2025) (“DOE Order”).
3
  16 U.S.C. § 824a(c).

                                                      1
 challenged by multiple parties outside of FERC in the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C.

Circuit. The IL OAG notes that the DOE Order exceeds DOE’s authority and is not supported by

substantial evidence, and the validity of the DOE Order affects the Commission’s authority to

impose costs on Illinois consumers.

        SIGE filed a complaint in this proceeding seeking a mechanism for the Company to obtain

rate recovery under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) for the costs of operating

Culley Unit 2, which was scheduled to cease operations on December 31, 2025. 4 SIGE essentially

requested the same recovery mechanism that was approved by FERC for Consumers Energy

Company for operation of the J.H Campbell Generating Plant (“Campbell Plant”). 5 That is

allocation via “load ratio share” of all costs for the continued operation of Culley Unit 2 across

MISO North and Central. The Commission accepted this in its March 19 Order. 6

        The Commission noted that “Parties also may take appropriate steps, such as requesting

rehearing in this proceeding, to preserve arguments that, if the DOE Order were to be modified,

then the Commission should require refunds or otherwise revisit its approach to matters in

connection with the DOE Order.” 7 The costs of running Culley Unit 2 allocated throughout MISO

north/central will be expensive, given that the unit was slated to retire. Should the DOE Order be

vacated, which the IL OAG has requested of the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals 8 the Commission’s

March 19 Order would be without a legal basis. The Commission would then need to create a

method for refunding ratepayers the costs of such an expensive unit.



4
  Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. EL26-38-000,
Complaint (filed January 5, 2026).
5
  Consumers Energy Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,158 (2025) (“Consumers Energy
Order”), order on reh’g, 193 FERC ¶ 61,228 (2025) (“Consumers Energy Rehearing Order”).
6
  Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,214 (2026)
(“March 19 Order”).
7
   March 19 Order at 15-16 (para. 38).
8
   See Sierra Club et. al v. U.S. Dept. of Energy (D.C. Cir. Case No. 26-1057 (consol. with 26-1076 and 26-1078)).

                                                        2
 II.        REQUEST FOR REHEARING

           A. Statement of Issues

      1. In its March 19 Order, the Commission erred in accepting the proposed cost-allocation
method, because it is not supported by substantial evidence in the record, ignores the obligations
of SIGE’s customers to pay SIGE rates for generation and delivery, and is inconsistent with the
FPA 202(c) requirement of just and reasonable rates. 9

        2. The Commission erred by declining to require MISO to initiate a stakeholder process
to ensure that ratepayers subject to the order have a forum to address cost allocation and to ensure
that rates are just and reasonable.

           B. Argument

           1. The Commission erred in accepting the proposed cost-allocation method because
              it is not supported by substantial evidence in the record, ignores the obligations of
              SIGE’s customers to pay SIGE rates for generation and delivery, and is
              inconsistent with the FPA 202(c) requirement of just and reasonable rates.

           In the Commission’s March 19 Order, the Commission granted SIGE’s proposed tariff,

which spreads costs across MISO’s north/central region without determining the reliability benefit

for those ratepayers. The March 19 Order, like the DOE Order, is not supported by substantial

evidence in the record. It fails to identify any reliability benefit that may be realized by customers

outside the SIGE territory associated with Culley Unit 2 and does not address how SIGE’s status

as a vertically integrated utility may affect cost allocation. Specifically, in allocating costs, the

Commission should consider more than load ratio within MISO’s North and Central region.

           There has been little to no opportunity for parties to assess the load ratio cost-allocation

mechanism adopted by the Commission as it relates to Culley Unit 2. The cost allocation method

should expressly consider whether either existing SIGE load or new, large load customers within

the SIGE service area are utilizing Culley Unit 2. The costs to keep Culley Unit 2 operating should

be allocated to those who benefit from the plant, assuming any benefit exists (which the IL OAG


9
    16 U.S.C § 824d(a).

                                                    3
 does not concede). Allocating those costs based on load ratio without regard to any benefits

provided by Culley Unit 2 is unfair, unjust, and unreasonable.

        The DOE order relied on by the Commission fails to identify the reliability benefits it

claims. 10 In allocating costs, the Commission should not perpetuate this error. Further, it is

inconsistent with the FPA 202(c) requirement of just and reasonable rates. 11 FERC must ensure

that cost recovery and cost allocation are just and reasonable, particularly when there are ratepayers

who are not benefiting from, nor causing, the costs.

        While the DOE Order does not reference the growth of large load customers who use more

than 50 megawatts of power, and that are responsible for much of the load growth in MISO as well

as in other regions like PJM, 12 the Commission should not adopt a cost allocation methodology

that ignores that large load customers may operate in the SIGE territory and take advantage of

Culley Unit 2. Customers who may benefit (under the assumption that there are any benefits at

all, which the IL OAG does not concede), including large load customers, should not be subsidized

by the rest of MISO North and Central customers by requiring MISO customers to cover the costs

of keeping Culley Unit 2 operating based on load ratio.

        Certain large load data center companies even signed a ratepayer protection pledge to

protect ratepayers from subsidizing their costs, pledging that these large loads will build, bring, or

buy their generation. 13 Thus, the Commission should consider whether Culley Unit 2 is being

retained to serve large load. Only customers who directly benefit (if there are any benefits, which

   March 19 Order at para. 4 (citing DOE Order).
11
   16 U.S.C § 824d(a).
12
   See, e.g., Catherine Boudreau, Indiana is getting $15 billion in Big Tech investment. Residents don't want to foot
the     energy     bill,  https://www.businessinsider.com/indiana-big-techs-ai-data-centers-energy-amazon-google-
microsoft-2025-2 (accessed April 20, 2026).
13
         Ratepayer       Protection     Pledge,        The        White      House       (March       4,      2026),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.

                                                         4
 the IL OAG does not concede) from Culley Unit 2, which could include new load, should be

allocated those costs.

         The FPA 202(c) requirement of just and reasonable rates encompasses the principle of cost-

causation, or that ratepayers who supposedly benefit from Culley Unit 2 should pay the costs to

keep Culley Unit 2 operating. 14 Consistent with what multiple parties have argued in this

proceeding, the cost-causation principle requires that “in order to ensure just and reasonable rates,

FERC must make some reasonable effort to match costs to benefits.” 15 The Commission should

grant rehearing in order to address this principle.

         2. The Commission erred by declining to require MISO to initiate a stakeholder
            process to ensure that ratepayers subject to the order have a forum to address
            cost allocation and to ensure that rates are just and reasonable.

         There are various stakeholders in MISO. Unlike Indiana and many other MISO states,

Illinois is one of the few regions that is not vertically integrated. In effect, this tariff is shifting

costs that are generally part of an integrated utility’s rates onto residents in other states that are

covered by MISO without regard to the needs of either Indiana or each state. The DOE Order does

not identify the reliability benefit associated with keeping Culley Unit 2 operating and only makes

general statements about reliability in MISO North and Central regions. In light of this lack of

specificity, it is critical that any cost allocation method adopted by the Commission incorporate




14
   16 U.S.C § 824d(a); Illinois Com. Comm'n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 2009) (“FERC is not authorized
to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its members derive no
benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.”)
15
   Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1263 (D.C. Cir. 2018). See also El Paso Elec. Co. v. FERC,
76 F.4th 352, 356 (5th Cir. 2023) (“The FPA requires that all rates and charges made, demanded, or received by any
public utility for or in connection with the transmission or sale of electric energy be just and reasonable. 16 U.S.C.S.
§ 824d(a). For decades, the FERC and the courts have understood this requirement to incorporate a cost-causation
principle.”); Long Island Power Auth. & Long Island Lighting Co. v. FERC, 27 F.4th 705, 709 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (citing
Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368 (D.C. Cir. 2004)) (cleaned up) (“To be just and
reasonable, rates must ‘reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for them.’ This
‘cost-causation principle’ requires ‘comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed or benefits
drawn by that party.’”).

                                                           5
 the opportunity to develop more detailed assessments of the benefits, if any, of keeping Culley

Unit 2 open for various MISO regions and customers, including in Indiana.

       FERC should order the stakeholder process to provide the opportunity for stakeholders to

assess costs and any benefits to ensure that the charges associated with the plant and cost allocation

are based on the principle of cost causation where the cost causers are the cost payers. FERC must

ensure that cost recovery and cost allocation are just and reasonable, particularly when there are

ratepayers who are not benefitting from, nor causing, the costs.

III.   CONCLUSION

       WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, the Office of the Illinois Attorney General

respectfully requests that the Commission grant rehearing.



                                       Respectfully submitted,
